'''''Leptodictyum riparium''''', commonly known as '''Kneiff's feathermoss''',<ref name=BBS>{{cite book|last=Edwards|first=Sean R.|date=2012|title=English Names for British Bryophytes|location=Wootton, Northampton|publisher=British Bryological Society|isbn=978-0-9561310-2-7|issn=0268-8034|series=British Bryological Society Special Volume|volume=5|edition=4}}</ref> '''streamside leptodictyum moss''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=LERI6|taxon=Leptodictyum riparium|accessdate=4 February 2016}}</ref>, '''stringy moss''', <ref>{{Cite web |title=''Leptodictyum riparium'', Tropico.com (archived) |url=https://tropica.com/en/plants/plantdetails/Leptodictyumriparium(003ETC)/28671 |access-date=2025-12-09 |archive-date=2025-12-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251209022605/https://tropica.com/en/plants/plantdetails/Leptodictyumriparium(003ETC)/28671 |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref>, or '''knapwort''',<ref name="Manual">{{cite book |last=De Thabrew |first=Vivian |date=2014 |title=A Manual of Water Plants |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vNyVAgAAQBAJ&dq=Leptodictyum+Riparium&pg=PA129 |publisher=[[AuthorHouse]] |page=129 |isbn=978-1491889282 |accessdate=October 11, 2015}}</ref> is a species of moss<ref>{{cite book |last=Whittaker |first=R. H. |date=2012 |title=Classification of Plant Communities |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yFr-CAAAQBAJ&dq=Leptodictyum+Riparium&pg=PA140 |publisher=[[Springer Publishing]] |page=140 |isbn=978-9400991835 |accessdate=October 11, 2015}}</ref> of cosmopolitan distribution. The only places it is not found are the [[Pacific Islands]] and [[Australia]].<ref name="Manual" /> It is commonly found growing in the lakes and rivers of Minnesota<ref>{{cite book |last=Acton |first=Q. Ashton |date=2013 |title=Issues in Global Environment—Biodiversity, Resources, and Conservation: 2013 Edition |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hUKvK6EqYFQC&dq=Leptodictyum+Riparium&pg=PA269 |publisher=[[ScholarlyEditions]] |page=269 |isbn=978-1490109633 |accessdate=October 11, 2015}}</ref> and is also present in [[Mexico]], [[Guatemala]], the [[Bahamas]], [[Cuba]], [[Jamaica]], [[Haiti]], the [[Dominican Republic]], [[Venezuela]], [[Peru]] and [[Brazil]].<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=gylFAQAAIAAJ&q=Leptodictyum+Riparium Flora Neotropica], [[The New York Botanical Garden]], 2003, pages 40-43</ref>

This moss has several different forms and can grow up to 30 cm. Its ovate leaves, which are in two rows, are often pointed at their apex.<ref name="Manual" /> ''Leptodictyum riparium'' has been found in an acidic mining lake and can live at a pH down to 1.6 in volcanic craters. It was once found with ''[[Eleocharis acicularis]]'' at a Canadian mining lake.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Geller |first1=Walter |last2=Scultze |first2=Martin |last3=Kleinmann |first3=Bob |last4=Wolkersdorfer |first4=Christian |date=2012 |title=Acidic Pit Lakes: The Legacy of Coal and Metal Surface Mines |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BRrPvDTNn9EC&dq=Leptodictyum+Riparium&pg=PA151 |publisher=Springer Publishing |page=151 |isbn=978-3642293849 |accessdate=October 11, 2015}}</ref> It is known to contain high levels of [[phosphate]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lichtfouse |first1=Eric |last2=Schwarzbauer |first2=Jan |last3=Didier |first3=Robert |date=2013 |title=Green Materials for Energy, Products and Depollution |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MMLHBAAAQBAJ&dq=Leptodictyum+Riparium&pg=PA435 |publisher=Springer Publishing |pages=424–435 |isbn=978-9400768369 |accessdate=October 11, 2015}}</ref>.  It has been reported that ''L. riparium'' tolerates a wide range of nutrient conditions and its population increases as [[ammonia]] increases.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hanson |first1=David T. |last2=Rice |first2=Steven K. |date=2013 |title=Photosynthesis in Bryophytes and Early Land Plants |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0YnHBAAAQBAJ&dq=Leptodictyum+Riparium&pg=PA213 |publisher=Springer Publishing |pages=211–213 |isbn=978-9400769885 |accessdate=October 11, 2015}}</ref>

''Leptodictyum riparium'' is known to be able to use [[artificial light]] to grow in places which are otherwise devoid of natural light, such as [[Crystal Cave (Wisconsin)|Crystal Cave]] in [[Wisconsin]].<ref name="Thatcher 1949">{{cite journal |last1=Thatcher |first1=Edward P. |title=Bryophytes of an Artificially Illuminated Cave |journal=The Bryologist |date=1949 |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=212–214 |doi=10.2307/3239480 |jstor=3239480 }}</ref>

It is an easy to grow moss that is also used in aquariums. In the aquarium trade it is one of at least two species traded under the common name "Stringy Moss", another being [[Drepanocladus|Drepanocladus aduncus]].
